title: Fair locks and waiting in a loop

questions.stem: Per this page, what do you gain and what do you pay when you build a `ReentrantLock` with `new ReentrantLock(true)` instead of the default?

options.text: The longest-waiting thread goes next, and overall throughput drops
options.says: The page says a fair lock serves the longest waiter first, so nobody starves, but the extra context switching lowers throughput.

options.text: A newly arriving thread goes next, and some waiters may starve
options.says: The page describes this barging as what the default non-fair lock does, which is how it gets its higher throughput.

options.text: The lock's current owner goes next, and reentrancy stops working
options.says: The page says both kinds of ReentrantLock are reentrant; the flag only changes the order in which waiting threads get the lock.

questions.stem: Per this page, why is `condition.await()` called inside `while (!ready)` rather than `if (!ready)`?

options.text: A thread can wake from its wait even though no thread called signal()
options.says: The page says a thread may return from await() without signal() being called (a spurious wakeup), so the predicate must be checked again in a loop.

options.text: A thread can wake from its wait without the lock and must retake it afterwards
options.says: The page says the woken thread must re-acquire the lock before returning from await(), so it already holds the lock when the loop test runs.

options.text: A thread can enter its wait without holding the lock that guards the flag
options.says: The page lists calling await() without holding the lock as a pitfall that throws IllegalMonitorStateException; the lock must be held first.

origin.section: Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them
